## Style

- Inline single-use values. A `let` earns its place only when the
  name carries meaning the expression lacks, the value is read more
  than once, or the subset REQUIRES a pin (a `dyn` value selected
  among arms, a Result-answering lambda — "The subset today" names
  each). Empty literals (`[]`, `{}`) infer inline in
  constructor fields — never bind them to a throwaway name. When a
  pin seems needed, probe before assuming.
- A state struct's impl is its VOCABULARY: the small verbs that
  read or write its tables (`speak`, `bind`, `mint`, `give`) live
  as methods, so drivers read as prose. The free state fns the

// The pool's size and directory, settled on first use. No pool when it's turned off, sized to
// nothing, or its directory can't be made.
static void pool_settled(void) {
    if (g_slot_count >= 0) return;
    g_slot_count = 0;
    const char* sized = getenv("AVRA_MEM_POOL_MB");
    int64_t bytes = sized && *sized ? (int64_t)atoll(sized) << 20 : machine_bytes() / 100 * POOL_PERCENT;
    const char* waits = getenv("AVRA_MEM_POOL_WAIT_MS");
    if (waits && *waits) g_wait_ms = atoll(waits);
    if (bytes <= 0) return;
    const char* placed = getenv("AVRA_MEM_POOL_DIR");
    if (placed && *placed) {

    g_slot_count = (int)(slots < 1 ? 1 : slots > MOST_SLOTS ? MOST_SLOTS : slots);
}

#!/bin/sh
# THE CENSUS BUILD: exact retain/release/list-write counts, and the
# callers that cause them. Counting costs ~8% of a run, so it never
# ships: a census compiler is built BESIDE build/avra, from a runtime
# compiled with -DAVRA_CENSUS, and the shipping runtime library is
# rebuilt on every exit.
#   sh tools/census.sh check packages/std-avrac
#
# THE SHIPPING COMPILER IS NEVER REMOVED. It builds the census
# compiler, so a census that deletes it first has nothing to build
# with, and every recovery that rebuilds needs the memory and disk the
# census run just spent.
#
# CENSUS_EDIT MEASURES A WARM EDIT: the command runs once cold to fill the store,
# then CENSUS_EDIT edits the tree, and only the run after it is counted.
#   CENSUS_EDIT='sh tools/db_measure/edit_literal.sh' sh tools/census.sh check packages/cli
#
# A CENSUS THAT PRINTS NO COUNTS FAILS. A check that examined nothing
# is not a check that passed: no `rc:` line means the binary carried no
# census, and the run exits 1 saying so.
# A cold run clears the tree's `.avra-cache`; the machine store lives there too, or "cold" would read the machine's rows.
export AVRA_CACHE_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)/.avra-cache"
# a store is copied, counted or emptied here between builds, so each build saves its own before it answers
export AVRA_STORE_KEPT_HERE=1
set -eu
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
: "${LLVM_PREFIX:=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm}"
export LLVM_PREFIX

# THE CENSUS COUNTS THE COMPILER'S OWN WORK, under a memory cap: the old path's check the net runs
# before the program layer's is not that work, and its memory with the layer's passes the cap.
export AVRA_PROGRAM_NET=0
census=build/avra.census
stores=.avra-cache.census-saved
suffix=.census-saved
named="$*"
restore() {
    make --no-print-directory build/libavra_runtime.a > /dev/null 2>&1 || \
        echo "census: the shipping runtime did NOT rebuild — run \`make build/libavra_runtime.a\`"
    rm -f packages/cli/src/main packages/cli/src/main.av.ll
#!/bin/sh
AVRA_RC_KINDS=1 exec /work/avra-kinds/build/avra-kb "$@"

# THE CENSUS COMPILER: the cli this tree builds, over a runtime compiled with -DAVRA_CENSUS, written

#
# THE BUILDER IS build/avra unless CENSUS_BUILDER names another: a layout rule is the BUILDING
# compiler's, so a census of a rule builds the census compiler with a compiler that has it.
set -eu
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

builder=${CENSUS_BUILDER:-build/avra}
[ -x "$builder" ] || { echo "census: no $builder to build the census compiler with — run \`make avra\` first"; exit 1; }
# A MADE BOX IS NAMED BY ITS CALLER'S CALLER, two frames up, which only frame pointers reach:
# macOS keeps them always, Linux only when asked, in the runtime and in every emitted fn.
counted="-DAVRA_CENSUS -fno-omit-frame-pointer"

P=/tmp/claude-0/-home-user/b7879055-7443-55b4-86e4-a7edea59339f/scratchpad/p3; mkdir -p $P; cat > $P/p3.av <<'E'
type S = { xs: List<int>, name: string }

fn first(s: S) -> List<int> { s.xs }

fn grown(s: S, n: int) -> int {
    mut a = first(s)
    a.push(n)
    a.length + s.xs.length
}

fn rebuilt(s: S, n: int) -> S {
    mut t = s
    t.xs = first(s).concat([n])
    t
}

fn run() -> string {
    mut total = 0
    for i in 0..200000 {
        let s = S { xs: [i, i + 1], name: "n${i}" }
        total = total + grown(s, i) + rebuilt(s, i).xs.length
    }
    "${total}"
}

fn arm_exit(ins: List<Ins>, from: int) -> ArmExit {
    mut depth = 0
    mut diverges = false
    mut j = from

        let step = ins[j]

        j = j + 1

    ArmExit { diverges: diverges, boundary: j }
}

<to_controller>lent-answers, in progress: the census found a real leak, which the attack test and the soundness proof missed. The census compiler that lent's builder compiled hit the 12 GB ceiling (0.53 G retains vs 0.11 G releases; Lexing.push cloned the token list per token). Two defects fixed: (1) a tmp register renumbered past the old count wasn't marked as owning nothing, so it was double-released (pinned as the new `nested` case in lent_answers); (2) inference ran on IR without unwinding exits, while the memory pass sees them (`flag unwinding` arms answer a dummy 0). The chain failed, so 20 bodies marked lent counted their answer as owned and callers never released it. answer_chain and the soundness re-derivation now skip unwound exits, and soundness gained `owned_lent`, a defect for a body whose marks lend while its answer is owned (the cross-body leak a per-body walk can't see). Sound check: 0 defects. Census rerunning; uncommitted until it's green.</to_controller>

The census is running with both fixes.

### 2026-11-19T12:59:21 AGENT
By-kind census, base vs lent: lent cut owned-read retains by 52 M (936 → 884 M), but the totals didn't move (2.530 → 2.528 G retains). So the lent machinery alone is noise. The cell case lives in `owned: yielded 0.572 G`, where `node_at`'s 169 M owned gets land; adjacent kinds are "a load that outlives its cell" 0.182 G and "stored in a cell" 0.202 G.

<to_controller>Cell-load design (5 lines):
1. Callee: a body whose answer projects the CURRENT VALUE of a cell reached from seat j (`self.nodes.get()[i]`) gets mark `lent_through_cell[j]`, inferred like `lent` (chain may pass one `Load` of a cell that rides an eligible seat).
2. Caller: such a call's answer is read as a plain view only if, from the call to the last read of the view and of everything derived from it, no step may write any cell: no `Store` to a cell, no cell-writing row (`writes`/`cell_unique`), and no `Call`/`CallPtr` except to a body marked `writes_no_cell`. Cells alias (two fields can hold one cell box), so any write kills; no call also means no fiber switch, so no other task can write. Otherwise it takes the owned twin, as today.
3. `writes_no_cell` is inferred bottom-up from the body's own steps plus its callees' marks; a cycle, `CallPtr` or `dyn` counts as a write.
4. Needed for either: lending THROUGH a call. `node_at` is reached via `store.expr(id)` / `stmt(id)`, so the chain must accept a call to a lending body. That and (3) make inference read CALLEE facts, which neither `consumed` nor `lent` do today: a new cross-body dependency in the program layer, the real cost.
5. Soundness re-derives the window per call site (any cell write inside a lent-through-cell view's life is a defect), and `owned_lent` stays.
Estimate (one-core census, base55 cli build): node_at's owned gets are 169 M retains + 169 M releases, about 5.6% of 6.0 G RC ops (6.7% of retains), all in `owned: yielded`. My sample of 25 `store.expr` sites: ~7 call-free (a scalar-payload match, `is`), ~9 call only a leaf projection method (`text_of`, `body_of`, `elems_of`), ~9 keep a box payload live into calls that write cells. So coverage is ~30% with a call-free window alone (~0.05 G retains + 0.05 G releases) and ~60–65% with leaf `writes_no_cell` (~0.11 G + 0.11 G, ~3.5% of RC ops). Provable: yes, locally per window. Cut: real but modest, and it costs a cross-body fact (4). Plan unless you say otherwise: build (4) + (1) + the call-free window on top of 8cdd9cee, measure, then add `writes_no_cell` only if the measurement holds the estimate.</to_controller>

### 2026-11-19T13:00:30 LEAD/USER
Lead: good design, but consider the paradox-collapse version first, because the window analysis pays a cross-body fact for 60% coverage. The arena is APPEND-ONLY: nodes are pushed and never replaced or removed. An element of a grow-only list stays alive for as long as the list does, WHATEVER is written meanwhile. A push may move the buffer, but the element box is held by the list, not by the buffer slot's address. So a read of an existing element from a grow-only holder is a view by its TYPE, with no window and no callee facts. It covers all ~25 sample sites, including the 9 that keep payloads live into writing calls, and the full 169M+169M.
Shape: a type that can only grow (e.g. core `Arena<T>`, or a grow-only Cell: push and read, no set, no set_at, no remove) whose `at(i)` answers a lent view, held by the receiver's own standing. The memory pass needs only "the holder outlives the view", which a borrowed `self` or seat already guarantees.
Check three things:

//! THE SEALED LAW: a type marked `@sealed` (`@std/meta`) is BUILT and
//! REWRITTEN in the module that declares it and nowhere else — no
//! literal fills it, no `Name(value)` converts into it, no record
//! literal, `with`, field write or variant constructs it. Every READ
//! stays transparent: a field, equality, a pattern, a method. So a checked
//! constructor the module exports is the type's one door, and a value
//! of the type anywhere is one that door answered.
use core.{ExprId, TypeId, DeclId, Type}
use diagnostics.{Voice, said_as}
use @std.errors.{Loc}

/// The declaration a nominal shape names; none for a structural one.
fn sealable(sh: Type) -> DeclId? {
    match sh { .Struct(d, _) or .Enum(d, _) or .App(d, _, _) -> d, rest -> null }
}

impl TypeCx {
    /// Whether `d` is sealed and this file's module is not the one
    /// that declares it.
    fn sealed_elsewhere(d: DeclId) -> bool {
        let decls = self.view.decls
        decls.is_sealed(d) &&
            decls.module_of(d) != decls.module_name(decls.file(self.view.file).module_id)
    }

    /// Whether building or rewriting a `ty` here breaks its seal —
    /// spoken when it does. `how` is the site's own label.
    mut fn seals(at: Loc?, ty: TypeId, how: string) -> bool {
        let d? = sealable(self.view.types.shape_of(ty)) else { return false }
        self.seals_decl(at, d, how)
    }

    /// `seals` for a site that holds the declaration itself.
    mut fn seals_decl(at: Loc?, d: DeclId, how: string) -> bool {
        if !self.sealed_elsewhere(d) { return false }
        self.sealed_built(at, self.view.decls.decl(d).name, self.view.decls.module_of(d), how)
        true
    }

//! A list that only grows.
use @std.meta.{identity, opaque}
use @std.relation.engine.{list_cell}

/// A LIST THAT ONLY GROWS: an element once pushed is held for as long as the list is, whatever is
/// pushed or replaced after it — a replaced element is retired, never dropped — so a read of one is
/// a view its holder keeps standing. Opaque: only this module reaches the cells, so no write the
/// list does not allow can happen anywhere. An identity: a copy grows the same list.
@opaque
@identity
export type Grown<T> = { items: Cell<List<T>>, retired: Cell<List<T>> }

/// A list holding nothing yet.
export fn grown<T>() -> Grown<T> { Grown { items: list_cell<T>(), retired: list_cell<T>() } }

/// A list holding `values` first, in a cell of its own.
export fn grown_of<T>(values: List<T>) -> Grown<T> { Grown { items: Cell.new(values), retired: list_cell<T>() } }

impl Grown {
    fn push(v: T) { self.items.push(v) }

    fn at(i: int) -> T { self.items.get()[i] }

    fn length() -> int { self.items.get().length }

    /// Element `i` is `v` now; the one it held is retired, so a read of it still stands.
    fn replaced(i: int, v: T) {
        self.retired.push(self.items.get()[i])
        self.items.set_at(i, v)
    }

    /// The elements as they stand, a list of their own.
    fn listed() -> List<T> { self.items.get() }
}
E

### 2026-11-19T13:27:49 RUN Bash [hmos5udb]
```
cd /work/avra-lent/packages/std-avrac/src/core/tests; grep -n 'new_arena\|export fn new_arena' ../*.av | head -3; cat > grown_test.av <<'E'
// A list that only grows lends a read of an element for as long as the list stands, whatever is
// pushed or replaced after it: every box here is made at run time, so a view that dangles reads a
// freed one, and the RC guard names it.
use @std.avrac.core.{Grown, grown, grown_of, new_arena}

type Leaf = { name: string, tags: List<string> }

fn leaf(n: int, at: string) -> Leaf { Leaf { name: "${at}${n}", tags: ["${at}t${n}", "${at}u${n}"] } }

fn filled_with(n: int) -> Grown<Leaf> {
    let g: Grown<Leaf> = grown()
    for i in 0..n { g.push(leaf(i, "a")) }
    g
}

/// The element read before `i` is replaced, read again after the replace and a hundred pushes.
fn read_past_replace(i: int) -> string {
    let g = filled_with(4)
    let old = g.at(i)
    let tags = old.tags
    g.replaced(i, leaf(i, "b"))
    for k in 0..100 { g.push(leaf(k, "c")) }
    "${old.name} ${tags[1]} ${g.at(i).name} ${g.length()}"
}

/// The element read before a replace of every element, each replaced twice.
fn read_past_rewrites() -> string {
    let g = filled_with(3)
    let first = g.at(0)
    let last = g.at(2)
    for round in 0..2 { for j in 0..3 { g.replaced(j, leaf(j, "r${round}")) } }
    "${first.name}${last.tags[0]} ${g.at(0).name}"
}

/// A copy grows the same list, and a read through either stands past a replace through the other.
fn read_through_copy() -> string {
    let g = filled_with(2)
    let h = g
    let seen = h.at(1)
    g.replaced(1, leaf(1, "d"))
    "${seen.name} ${h.at(1).name}"
}

/// An arena's node read before the node is replaced, and before the arena forks and the fork replaces it.
fn arena_node_past_replace() -> string {
    let a = new_arena<Leaf>()
    for i in 0..3 { let _ = a.add(leaf(i, "e"), null) }
    let before = a.node_at(1)
    a.replaced(1, leaf(1, "f"))
    let forked = a.forked()
    let mid = forked.node_at(1)
    forked.replaced(1, leaf(1, "g"))
    "${before.name} ${mid.name} ${a.node_at(1).name} ${forked.node_at(1).name}"
}

spec "core/grown" {
    given "a read of an element" {
        then "stands past a replace of it and pushes that move the list" {
            read_past_replace(1) == "a1 at1 b1 104" && read_past_replace(0) == "a0 au0 b0 104"
        }
        then "stands past every element replaced twice" {
            read_past_rewrites() == "a0at2 r10"
        }
        then "through a copy stands past a replace through the original" {
            read_through_copy() == "a1 d1"
        }
        then "of an arena's node stands past its replace and a fork's" {
            arena_node_past_replace() == "e1 f1 f1 g1"
        }
    }
    given "a list that only grows" {
        then "holds what it was given first" {
            let g = grown_of([leaf(0, "h"), leaf(1, "h")])
            g.push(leaf(2, "h"))
            g.length() == 3 && g.at(0).name == "h0" && g.listed()[2].name == "h2"
        }
    }
}
E

A list that only grows lends a read of its element: Grown, @opaque, and an outlasting view

`Grown<T>` (core/grown.av) pushes, reads and replaces, and a replaced element is retired, never
dropped, so an element once read stands as long as the list does whatever is written after.
`@opaque` (`@std/meta`) keeps that a law of the type: sealed, and its fields are read only in the
module that declares it — refused on both checkers (`type.opaque`). A `Grown`'s element read is
known by its symbol and lends from its receiver through its cell; a body reading it directly
lends too, its view marked `outlasts`, and a caller reads that view through `avra_grown_view`,
which no call changes — only what lets the holder go: its release, or a call taking it, or a box
it rides, into a consuming seat. The arena's nodes are a `Grown` now, and a store's `expr` and
`stmt` read them directly.

**The classifier** is what makes candidates automatic. A census site's SHAPE names its technique:

| site shape (from the census) | technique |
|---|---|
| a box freed in the fn that made it | stack records (escape analysis) |
| a free at rc 1 followed by an alloc of the same size | reuse in place |
| a retain whose release is the binding's last use | move at last use |
| `avra_streq`/name compare callers | interned names |
| a box of flat scalar fields pushed into a list | strided list |
| a slot box over a crossed box (`F?`) | nullable flat record |
| a list made and only walked once | deforestation |
| an indirect call whose target set is one fn | devirtualization |
| a `dyn` box laid with N code pointers | static method tables |

`avra census --candidates` prints the top sites per technique with their counts and the source
line, so a ranked work list is one command. Run per batch on the gate's workloads, its output
diffed against the last run is how a NEW candidate appears without anyone looking.

## How work is assessed

- **Every PR**: the exact-count gate holds; a new shape-rule finding fails like an idiom.
- **Every new feature**: its design post names its cost (boxes, calls, copies per use) and which
  registry rows it relies on or adds. A feature that makes idiomatic code slower needs a row that
  removes the cost, or it is not ready.
- **Maintenance**: a finding from any detector is a row or a ticket at discovery, never a comment.
- **New techniques** join this tab

/// Whether a gathering of `kind` takes `d`: a declaration wearing its mark, or an instance of its
/// component.
fn takes_member(engine: QueryEngine, kind: CollectKind, d: DeclaredName) -> bool {
    match kind {
        .Annotated(mark) -> wears_mark(engine, d, mark),
        .Component(word) -> instances_word(engine, d, word),
    }
}

/// What `file` declares: what it writes, then what generators make there when `made`. Absent where a
/// generator there isn't made, so what it declares isn't known.
fn declared_in(engine: QueryEngine, file: SourceFileAddress, made: bool) -> List<DeclaredName>? {
    let written = file_declares(engine, file).names
    if !made { return written }
    if !generators_made(engine, file) { return null }
    written.concat(generated_declares(engine, file).names)
}

/// Whether a gathering written in `owner` reads `file`'s members: any file outside a module's tests,

fn gathers_from(file: SourceFileAddress, owner: SourceFileAddress) -> bool {
    !module_segments(file).contains(TESTS_DIR) || spelled_file(file) == spelled_file(owner)
}

/// type that isn't an enum the program declares.
fn enum_shape(engine: QueryEngine, ty: SignedType) -> EnumShape? {
    let at? = declared_at(ty) else { return null }
    let declared? = enum_signature(engine, at.file, at.name) else { return null }
    EnumShape { params: declared.type_params.length, variants: declared.variants }
}

    let at? = declared_at(ty) else { return null }
    let record? = record_signature(engine, at.file, at.name) else { return null }
    RecordShape { params: record.type_params.length, fields: record.fields }

/// A component's signature as a record's: its type parameters with their bounds, and its fields — its head's, then each
/// member as the field that holds it, an event's the nullable fn its handler is, in order, then what
/// it carries.
fn component_signature(engine: QueryEngine, file: SourceFileAddress, item: ReadItem, name: string) -> RecordSignature? {
    let s? = item.stmts.find((s) -> item.store.component_parts(s)?.name == name) else { return null }
    let parts = item.store.component_parts(s)!
    let signing = signing_in(engine, file, parts.tparams)
    let own = [field_seat(engine, signing, p) for p in parts.head.concat(parts.holders)]
    carrying(engine, file, item, name, parts.tparams, own) with { bounds: signing.bounds_written(item.store.decl_tbounds(s)) }
}

# One run of the census compiler in the snapshot, once what it reads is older than the stamp window:
# its census to <name>.out, what it printed to <name>.stdout.
counted() {
    name=$1; shift
    sleep 3
    started=$(date +%s)
    # the census reports at exit only where the run accounts (AVRA_MEM_STATS)
    (cd "$src" && AVRA_MEM_STATS=1 AVRA_WORK_AHEAD_OFF=1 AVRA_PROGRAM_NET=0 AVRA_CACHE_DIR="$cache" AVRA_STORE_KEPT_HERE=1 \

    echo "cost: $name $(($(date +%s) - started)) s"
}

# One warm findings run of the cli, its `worked:` line kept as <name>.out, its census beside it.

#!/bin/sh
# THE CENSUS COMPILER: the cli this tree builds, over a runtime compiled with -DAVRA_CENSUS, written
# to <out>. It counts exactly what the shipping compiler does and never ships: the shipping runtime
# library is rebuilt before this answers, and the cli's own product is gone.
#   sh tools/census_compiler.sh build/avra.census
#
# THE BUILDER IS build/avra unless CENSUS_BUILDER names another: a layout rule is the BUILDING
# compiler's, so a census of a rule builds the census compiler with a compiler that has it.
set -eu
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
out=${1:-build/avra.census}
builder=${CENSUS_BUILDER:-build/avra}
[ -x "$builder" ] || { echo "census: no $builder to build the census compiler with — run \`make avra\` first"; exit 1; }
# A MADE BOX IS NAMED BY ITS CALLER'S CALLER, two frames up, which only frame pointers reach:
# macOS keeps them always, Linux only when asked, in the runtime and in every emitted fn.
counted="-DAVRA_CENSUS -fno-omit-frame-pointer"
shipping() {
    make --no-print-directory build/libavra_runtime.a > /dev/null 2>&1 || \
        echo "census: the shipping runtime did NOT rebuild — run \`make build/libavra_runtime.a\`"
    find packages/cli/src/main packages/cli/src/main.av.ll -maxdepth 0 -delete 2> /dev/null || :
}
trap shipping EXIT INT TERM
make --no-print-directory CFLAGS_avra_runtime="$counted" CFLAGS_avra_hot="$counted" build/libavra_runtime.a > /dev/null

//! Typed values over the query kernel. A family owns one memo; copies
//! share both its database and its value table, so higher-order query
//! bodies may safely capture either handle.
extern fn avra_qtrace(line: string)

export enum MemoAsk<T> {
    Reuse(T)
    Compute
    Cycle
}

impl ContentHash {
    /// The hash as one text, what a table of what its answer reads back as is keyed by.
    fn held_key() -> string { "${self.high_word}:${self.low_word}" }

    /// An order over hashes, for keeping them sorted.
    fn comes_before(other: ContentHash) -> bool {
        self.high_word < other.high_word ||
            self.high_word == other.high_word && self.low_word < other.low_word
    }

    fn same_as(other: ContentHash) -> bool { self.high_word == other.high_word && self.low_word == other.low_word }
}

/// The hash of `octets`.

#!/bin/sh
# THE EXACT-COUNT GATE'S MEASUREMENT: the census compiler of this tree, run over FIXED workloads whose
# sources are one pinned commit (the `snapshot` row of tools/cost.baseline): cold, each run's census
# kept as build/cost/<workload>.out; and warm after each edit of a fixed set, the answers it worked out
# again kept as build/cost/edit-<kind>.out. tools/cost_ratchet.py judges them.
#   sh tools/cost.sh                      the baseline's snapshot
#   COST_SNAPSHOT=<sha> sh tools/cost.sh  another snapshot (what `make cost-accept` records)
#   COST_COMPILER=<file> sh tools/cost.sh a census compiler already built from this tree
#
# A FIXED INPUT MEASURES THE COMPILER: the snapshot is exported whole, std included, and the census
# compiler stands at its build/avra beside the objects a build links, so every package it reads is

# ONE PROCESS ON ONE CORE DOES ALL THE WORK: a forked worker's counts are its own, so no body is

//! A FN'S CODE HASH (`@std/meta`'s `code_hash`): what its lowered code
//! does, and everything it can reach, as one key — never a comment or a
//! span. It sums a digest of each node the fn reaches (`summed_hash`), so
//! an edit moves exactly the hashes reaching it, by its node's digest
//! alone. A name is part of a node, so a rename moves the hashes that
//! reach it. A call THROUGH a fn value reaches every fn
//! whose address the program takes WITH THAT FN TYPE, so the callee it
//! cannot name is covered by TYPE, never by the whole program's values.
//! EVERY REFERENCE LIST IS POSITIONAL — a body's in the order its
//! instructions name them, a static's in slot order —
//! but the fn values', a set, since a value dispatches by address.
//!
//! A TYPE IS ITS SHAPE, so a renamed type or field moves nothing — sound
//! only while no name reaches output except through the IR: a record has

### 2026-11-19T20:53:34 AGENT
Found the mechanism, pending the control.

- **Input checks** (query_engine.av:546): `frontier_opened` checks the standing inputs in place order.
- **Cut decisions** (query_engine.av:604-627): `suspects_of` calls `f.readers_of(changed, cut_at)` and settles each cutting answer in place order.
- **Place order is question-hash order** (frontier.av:836-854). A question's hash includes its code hash.

So whichever cutting question comes first in hash order computes the shared reads, such as `file_scope` against `file_items`, and its record owns them. That changes what the next edit reaches. Waiting on base56 v3 and v4 to see whether this predates lent.

<to_controller>A/B with `Q ask`: adding the line again made B 280 (A 280, B 280). The ask order differs, though: the first root asks are A [language_print, source_text, file_scope→computes file_items] and B [source_text, language_print, file_items computed as a root]. The mechanism: the frontier checks its inputs (frontier_opened) and decides its cuts (suspects_of → readers_of → cut_at) in place order, and place order is question-hash order (frontier.av places_in_order / sorted_by_hash). A question's hash includes the code hash of the lowered code its query reaches. So any change in reachable lowered code reorders the cut decisions. That changes which question computes a shared read and owns it in its record, and so what a later edit reaches: 280 vs 286. The lent reorder changes lowered code, and so does every probe I add, which is why the probes flip it. The base56 control could not see this: an unused fn is not reached, and swapping two whole fns leaves the digest the same, so no hash moved. Running the proper control now: base56 with equivalent edits that do move hashes (disjunct order inside `closes` and `turns`, which are reached). I expect the defect predates lent: warm `worked` depends on code-hash order.</to_controller>

### 2026-11-19T20:54:33 AGENT
The order dependence is in `Frontier.readers_of` (frontier.av:448-477). It's a stack walk that marks a place `reached` the first time it pops. A reader met first from a merely suspect place is pushed undecided and never gets `decide` (so it never cuts), and its readers inherit "suspect". Met first from a moved place, the same reader is decided: if it stands it cuts, if it moved its readers get decided too. Both the suspect set and the cut work done therefore depend on pop order, which is place order, which is hash order.

<to_controller>Design for the frontier fix (control still running):
(1) The order dependence is in `Frontier.readers_of` (frontier.av:448): its DFS stack marks a place reached on first pop. A reader first met from a merely suspect place is never decided; met first from a moved place, it is decided and may cut. So the suspect set and the cut work (counted in `worked`) follow pop order, which is place order, which is hash order.
(2) Fix: two passes. First the plain reader closure of `changed`, ignoring cuts. Then a walk of that closure in topological order (Kahn: a place goes only after every read of it inside the closure is settled), so each place sees the final state of all its reads.
(3) Canonical rule per place r: if r has at least one moved read (changed or CUT_MOVED) and its query cuts, decide(r). STANDS means r is not a suspect, because it was just worked fresh. MOVED means suspect and moved. Otherwise, if any read is a suspect, r is a suspect without being decided. Same graph and same answers give the same set and the same decide calls, whatever the order.
(4) The tie-break among ready places is by place only for determinism, and the result can't depend on it. Who computes a shared child first then changes nothing recorded (one compute, the same reads), so `worked` is fixed.
(5) Proof: a std-program test running readers_of on a permuted copy of one graph and asserting the same reached set and decide set; then A/B and probe variants with identical `worked` on every edit row, plus the warm-row cost gate. Any difference against today is a narrower suspect set (fewer reworks), never a wider one.</to_controller>

file_path: /work/avra/packages/std-program/src/tests/frontier_order_test.av
--- content ---
// THE FRONTIER'S ORDER IS NOT ITS WORK: a frontier keeps its places in the order of their questions'
// hashes, and a question's hash moves with its query's code. One graph of queries, built under several
// spellings of its code, is several orders of the same places; a warm process after one edit must
// work out the same answers, and the same set of them, under every one, and answer what a cold
// process answers. Separate stores over one directory stand in for separate processes.
use @std.io.{make_dirs}
use @std.text.{parse_int}
use @std.time.{stamp}
use answer_record.{question}
use disk_store.{disk_store_at}
use query_engine.{QueryDefinition, QueryEngine, query_engine}
use sorted.{sorted_by}

/// What `name` answers about `argument`, asked as this binary asks it.
fn asked(e: QueryEngine, name: string, argument: string) -> string {
    e
        .answer_to(question(name, e.definitions.get().get(name)!.code_hash, argument.bytes()))
        .copied()
        .text() ?? ""
}

/// A query of `code`, cutting where `cuts` says.
fn query(name: string, code: string, cuts: bool, compute: fn(QueryEngine, Bytes) -> Bytes) -> QueryDefinition {
    QueryDefinition { query_name: name, code_hash: code, is_input: false, cuts: cuts, compute: compute }
}

/// `text` reads the world. `length` cuts and moves with any edit that changes a length; `echo`
/// repeats the text and doesn't cut, so an edit only reaches past it. `measured` cuts, reads both and
/// moves with the length; `steady` cuts and only says whether it's past zero, which stands; `shown`
/// reads `steady`. `through` cuts, and a change reaches it ONLY through `echo`, a place merely
/// reached: it must be worked out again all the same.
fn binary(code: string, world: Map<string, string>) -> List<QueryDefinition> {
    [
        QueryDefinition {
            query_name: "text",
            code_hash: code,
            is_input: true,
            compute: (_e, a) -> (world.get(a.text() ?? "") ?? "").bytes(),
        },
        query("length", code, true, (e, a) -> "${asked(e, "text", a.text() ?? "").length}".bytes()),
        query("echo", code, false, (e, a) -> asked(e, "text", a.text() ?? "").bytes()),
        query(
            "measured",
            code,
            true,
            (e, a) -> "${asked(e, "length", a.text() ?? "")}:${asked(e, "echo", a.text() ?? "").length > 0}".bytes(),
        ),
        query(
            "steady",
            code,
            true,
            (e, a) -> "${(parse_int(text_until(asked(e, "measured", a.text() ?? ""), ":")) ?? 0) > 0}".bytes(),
        ),
        query("shown", code, false, (e, a) -> "shown ${asked(e, "steady", a.text() ?? "")}".bytes()),
        query("through", code, true, (e, a) -> "${asked(e, "echo", a.text() ?? "").length}".bytes()),
    ]
}

/// The text of `s` before the first `stop`, all of it where there's none.
fn text_until(s: string, stop: string) -> string {
    let at = s.index_of(stop) ?? s.length
    s.substring(0, at)
}

/// Every path's answers the roots give, one line.
fn answers(e: QueryEngine) -> string {
    ["${asked(e, "shown", p)} ${asked(e, "through", p)} ${asked(e, "measured", p)}" for p in PATHS].join(" | ")
}

const PATHS: List<string> = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]

fn world(edited: bool) -> Map<string, string> {
    {"a": if edited { "abcd" } else { "abc" }, "b": "xy", "c": if edited { "q" } else { "pp" }, "d": "zzzz"}
}

/// One process of the binary spelled `code` over `directory` in `world`: its answers, then what it
/// worked out, sorted, so an order can't tell two runs apart.
type Ran = { answers: string, worked: string }

fn ran(directory: string, code: string, edited: bool) -> Ran {
    let store = disk_store_at(directory)
    let engine = query_engine(store, binary(code, world(edited)))
    let said = answers(engine)
    engine.frontier_kept()
    let _ = store.saved()
    Ran { answers: said, worked: sorted_by(engine.computed_queries(), (x, y) -> x < y).join(",") }
}

/// The warm process after the edit, over a store a cold process in the unedited world left.
fn warm_after_edit(code: string) -> Ran {
    let directory = "/tmp/avra-frontier-order/${stamp()}-${code}"
    let _ = make_dirs(directory) catch ""
    let _ = ran(directory, code, false)
    ran(directory, code, true)
}

/// What a cold process answers in the edited world.
fn cold_edited(code: string) -> string {
    let directory = "/tmp/avra-frontier-order/${stamp()}-cold-${code}"
    let _ = make_dirs(directory) catch ""
    ran(directory, code, true).answers
}

/// The spellings of the code: each is another order of the same places.
const CODES: List<string> = ["c1", "c2", "c3", "k7", "q9", "zz", "m4", "w0"]

spec "frontier — its order is not its work" {
    given "one graph under eight orders" {
        then "every order works out the same set of answers after one edit" {
            let worked = [warm_after_edit(c).worked for c in CODES]
            worked.all(it == worked[0])
        }
        then "every order answers what a cold process answers" {
            CODES.all((c) -> warm_after_edit(c).answers == cold_edited(c))
        }
        then "a change that reaches a cut only through a place merely reached still works it out" {
            let warm = warm_after_edit("c1")
            warm.answers.contains("shown true 4 4:true") && warm.worked.split(",").contains("through")
        }
    }
}

```
/// One process of the binary spelled `code` over `directory` in `world`: its answers, then what it
/// worked out, counted by query, so an order can't tell two runs apart.
type Ran = { answers: string, worked: string }

fn ran(directory: string, code: string, edited: bool) -> Ran {
    let store = disk_store_at(directory)
    let engine = query_engine(store, binary(code, world(edited)))
    let said = answers(engine)
    engine.frontier_kept()
    let _ = store.saved()
    let worked = engine.computed_queries()
    Ran {
        answers: said,
        worked: ["${n}:${worked.filter(it == n).length}" for n in NAMES].join(","),
    }
}

/// The warm process after the edit, over a store a cold process in the unedited world left.
fn warm_after_edit(code: string) -> Ran {
    let directory = "/tmp/avra-frontier-order/${stamp()}-${code}"
    let _ = make_dirs(directory) catch ""
    let _ = ran(directory, code, false)
    ran(directory, code, true)
}

frontier: settle a change's readers in reading order, never hash order

readers_of walked a stack in place order, and a frontier keeps its places
in the order of their questions' hashes, which move with any change to the
lowered code a query reaches. A reader met first from a merely reached
place went undecided; met first from a moved place it was decided and could
cut. So the suspect set, and the warm work it costs, moved with unrelated
compiler changes: the warm lane's edit-added row read 280 or 286 between
two equivalent sources.

Now every place the change can reach is found first, then each is settled
once every place it reads among them is settled: decided when it read a
moved place, reached undecided when it read only reached ones. The set
reached and the set decided are one function of the graph and the answers.

frontier_order_test: one graph under eight code spellings (eight place
orders) reaches the same places and works out the same answers, each equal
to a cold process's; a cut a change reaches only through a merely reached
place is still worked out. Against the old walk it reaches 12 or 14 by
order; now 10 under every order.

A place that read a moved place is decided: STANDS cuts it, MOVED reaches it and marks it moved, NOT_CUT reaches it. A place that read only reached places is reached undecided. target=std-json

}

The only rows `Q ask` itself explains are `once: 598 → 599 reads, 1369 → 1375 pointer compares`: the flag is read once and checked at its sites. ### 2026-11-20T04:40:32 AGENT
I have the full mechanism. `digest_of_binary` (build.av:416) does `read_bytes(at)` on the whole ~100 MB binary and digests it in memory. So any run whose compiler binary was written within 2 s holds the binary on the heap, and the next run repeats it until one run outside the window writes the record. That explains the 190 MB. It also explains the tracked `packages/cli/src/.main.print` that moved during the gate: it is this record, stamp plus absolute path plus digest, beside the cli's own built binary.

<to_controller>The 190 MB first-edit spike is explained, deterministic and pre-existing.
- **Repro:** place a compiler (`cp X build/avra.new && mv …`, a new file), run a cold check within 2 s, then an edited check. The edited check peaks at 190 MB every time. With a 3 s wait after placing the binary: 9 MB, every time (9/190/9, 190/9/190/9).
- **Mechanism:** `own_print` (cli disk_host.av:166) keys every kept artifact by a digest of the compiler binary's bytes. It caches that digest in a record beside the binary, keyed by the binary's stamp. Inside the 2 s window `stamp()` withholds, so the run digests the bytes and writes no record, and the next run digests again. `digest_of_binary` (std-avrac build.av:416) does `read_bytes` on the whole ~100 MB binary, which is the peak.
- **What's wrong:** the re-read itself is the stated design ("the bytes are read again when … the host cannot tell"). Holding the binary on the heap isn't necessary.
- **Proposed fix (batch 59, small):** digest the binary through a mapping, std-program already has `avra_mmap_open`, or stream it in chunks. The window case then costs a read, not ~190 MB live. Witness: the repro above, with peak live within noise of the 3 s case.
- **Related:** the tracked `packages/cli/src/.main.print` that the gate rewrote is this very record (stamp, absolute path, digest) for the cli's own built binary. It shouldn't be tracked; I suggest untracking and ignoring it in the same change.
- **Status:** Q ask's four-build spread is still running. Shall I take the mmap digest for 59?</to_controller>

/// What a digest has seen so far, as octets the C reads back. The octets
/// are the C's working state, not a canonical form: two hashers that saw
/// the same input may hold different octets, and the layout may change
/// with the vendored C — never compare them, and never persist them.
export type Hasher = { state: Bytes }

impl Hasher {
    /// The hasher that has also seen `b`.
    fn update(b: Bytes) -> Hasher {
        Hasher {

    /// The digest of everything seen: 32 octets. The hasher stands, and
    /// more input may follow.
    fn digest() -> Bytes { held(avra_b3_digest(self.state, self.state.length), DIGEST_LEN) }

    /// `digest`, as 64 lowercase hex characters.
    fn digest_hex() -> string { texted(avra_b3_digest_hex(self.state, self.state.length)) }

    A value of parts is held and passed as its leaves; a level-0 object answers one through a lent pointer

    Every pack keeps its tables' slots: a lookup probes, never searches
    
    A lookup searched each mapped pack in turn, a binary search over its keys' high
    words, and a miss searched them all: 11.3 of the bodies wave's 94.7 CPU-s. A
    pack's index now holds, beside each table, an open-addressed table of its
    entries' places by their keys' high words, a power of two at least twice their
    count, written at every save and merge; a lookup walks from the key's slot to
    the key or a free slot. The seal is avrapak7; a pack sealed avrapak6 is still

- **Peak:** over 5,242,880 bytes, since the old path refuses it at the 5 MiB default; within 10 MiB, since the program layer accepts it under std-avrac's lift.
- **Why it matters:** base57's Seating, one variant fewer, fits under 5 MiB, so the derive sits right at the line and grows with each variant.
- **Open question:** why one enum's codec derive holds megabytes; my guess is that it keeps every variant's quoted code until it answers.
Keeping `.Opaque`. lent-59 is building with AVRA_PROGRAM_NET=0, and I'll keep testing that way until 58 lands.</to_controller>

file_path: /work/avra/tools/grown_read_witness.sh
--- content ---
#!/bin/sh
# A GROW-ONLY HOLDER LENDS BY WHAT IT IS, NEVER BY ITS NAME: a holder written here, wearing nothing but
# `@opaque` and `@std/meta`'s `@grown_read`, lends its element read, and its caller reads the answer as
# a grown view (`avra_grown_view` in the caller's IR). The same holder without the mark, or with the
# mark on a type that is not `@opaque`, lends nothing. Every spelling prints what it prints natively
# under the evaluator too.
#   sh tools/grown_read_witness.sh [compiler]   (default build/avra)
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
avra=${1:-build/avra}
[ -x "$avra" ] || { echo "grown_read_witness: no compiler at $avra" >&2; exit 1; }
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'find "$tmp" -delete' EXIT

# The holder, spelled with `$1` before its type and `$2` before its element read.
holder() {
    cat << EOF
use @std.meta.{grown_read, identity, opaque}

$1
@identity
type Shelf<T> = { items: Cell<List<T>>, retired: Cell<List<T>> }

fn shelf<T>() -> Shelf<T> { Shelf { items: Cell.new([]), retired: Cell.new([]) } }

impl Shelf {
    fn put(v: T) { self.items.push(v) }
    $2
    fn get_at(i: int) -> T { self.items.get()[i] }
    fn swapped(i: int, v: T) {
        self.retired.push(self.items.get()[i])
        self.items.set_at(i, v)
    }
}

type Book = { title: string, pages: List<string> }

fn title_length(s: Shelf<Book>, i: int) -> int { s.get_at(i).title.length }

let s: Shelf<Book> = shelf()
for k in 0..3 { s.put(Book { title: "b\${k}", pages: ["p\${k}"] }) }
let before = s.get_at(1)
s.swapped(1, Book { title: "swapped", pages: [] })
println("\${title_length(s, 0)} \${before.title} \${s.get_at(1).title} \${title_length(s, 1)}")
EOF
}

failed=0
check() {
    name=$1; want_view=$2
    f="$tmp/$name.av"
    holder "$3" "$4" > "$f"
    "$avra" ir "$f" > "$tmp/$name.ir" 2>&1 || { echo "grown_read_witness: $name: ir failed"; tail -5 "$tmp/$name.ir"; failed=1; return; }
    # the caller's own fn, from its header to the next one
    views=$(awk '/title_length/ && /fn|define|^[^ ]/ { on = 1 } on && /avra_grown_view/ { n++ } on && /^}/ { on = 0 } END { print n + 0 }' "$tmp/$name.ir")
    "$avra" run "$f" > "$tmp/$name.native" 2>&1
    "$avra" run --eval "$f" > "$tmp/$name.eval" 2>&1
    said=$(cat "$tmp/$name.native")
    if [ "$said" != "2 b1 swapped 7" ]; then echo "grown_read_witness: $name printed '$said'"; failed=1; fi
    if ! cmp -s "$tmp/$name.native" "$tmp/$name.eval"; then echo "grown_read_witness: $name: eval differs from native"; failed=1; fi
    if [ "$want_view" = yes ] && [ "$views" -eq 0 ]; then echo "grown_read_witness: $name: the caller reads no grown view"; failed=1; fi
    if [ "$want_view" = no ] && [ "$views" -ne 0 ]; then echo "grown_read_witness: $name: the caller reads a grown view it was never lent"; failed=1; fi
    echo "grown_read_witness: $name: $views grown view(s) in the caller, '$said' native and eval"
}

check marked yes "@opaque" "@grown_read"
check unmarked no "@opaque" ""
check open_type no "" "@grown_read"
exit $failed

#!/bin/sh
# THE CENSUS BUILD: exact retain/release/list-write counts, and the
# callers that cause them. Counting costs ~8% of a run, so it never
# ships: a census compiler is built BESIDE build/avra, from a runtime
# compiled with -DAVRA_CENSUS, and the shipping runtime library is
# rebuilt on every exit.
#   sh tools/census.sh check packages/std-avrac
#
# THE SHIPPING COMPILER IS NEVER REMOVED. It builds the census
# compiler, so a census that deletes it first has nothing to build
# with, and every recovery that rebuilds needs the memory and disk the
# census run just spent.
#
# CENSUS_EDIT MEASURES A WARM EDIT: the command runs once cold to fill the store,
# then CENSUS_EDIT edits the tree, and only the run after it is counted.
#   CENSUS_EDIT='sh tools/db_measure/edit_literal.sh' sh tools/census.sh check packages/cli
#
# A CENSUS THAT PRINTS NO COUNTS FAILS. A check that examined nothing
# is not a check that passed: no `rc:` line means the binary carried no
# census, and the run exits 1 saying so.

#define AVRA_BOX_H

#include <stdint.h>

// A box's KIND decides how it reclaims and clones: 0 a plain
// allocation, 1 an array, 2 a map, 3 a string, 4 octets. Below zero it is not
// counted: STATIC is immortal, DEAD is the guard's mark on a
// reclaimed box.
enum { KIND_DEAD = -2, KIND_STATIC = -1, KIND_PLAIN = 0, KIND_ARRAY = 1, KIND_MAP = 2, KIND_STR = 3, KIND_BYTES = 4 };

// AN IMMORTAL BOX KEEPS ITS SHAPE. A `once` answer and a static
// aggregate live for the process, so retain and release must no-op
// on them — which the `kind < 0` test already gives free — but
// `box_clone` still has to know whether one is a MAP, because a
// write through a shared value CLONES it, and a map cloned as an
// array is memory corruption. Overwriting the kind with KIND_STATIC
// loses exactly that. So immortality is a REFLECTION of the kind and
// never a replacement: negative for every shape, and it decodes back.
#define KIND_IMMORTAL(k) (-((k) + 4))
#define IS_IMMORTAL(k)   ((k) <= -4)
#define KIND_SHAPE(k)    (IS_IMMORTAL(k) ? -(k) - 4 : (k))

// A cell's mark bits (AvraArray.marks).
enum { MARK_OWNED = 1, MARK_ABSENT = 2, MARK_FRAME = 4 };

// "AVRA" — the bytes that say a header is this runtime's.

--- content ---
# Per-query regions for the compiler: design

Status: design only, no code. Source facts are cited by file and line (tree at lent-59 / base57).
Trigger: wrong-answers' measurement on a cold `check packages/cli`. 90.3% of its 816 M boxes (89% of
bytes) die inside the query that made them, and 58% of all retains and releases fall on those boxes.
The escapes are answers, tapes, store segments and table cells. Top escape sites: `array_clone`
(4.66 M), `SyntaxArena.placed_span`, `SavedLayoutWriter.finished`, `texts_of`, `Segment.keep`.

## 0. What the runtime and the engine give us today

- **The header.** A box carries a 16-byte header `{ tag, kind_word, rc, len }` (runtime/avra_box.h:40).
  Its kind is a signed byte: 0 plain, 1 array, 2 map, 3 string, 4 octets. A negative kind is
  uncounted. `KIND_STATIC` = −1 and `KIND_DEAD` = −2. `KIND_IMMORTAL(k)` = −(k+4) keeps the shape:
  −4..−8 are the five shapes, immortal. The kind byte's eight negative values are all spoken for
  except −3.
- **The hot leaves.** `avra_rc_retain` returns on `avra_kind(h) < 0` before it touches `rc`
  (avra_hot.c:12), and `avra_rc_release` returns there too, after its null and guard checks. An
  uncounted box costs one compare.
- **Uniqueness drives writes.** In-place writes and appends are licensed by `h->rc == 1`
  (avra_runtime.c:1612, 3936). A write through a shared value clones it (avra_box.h:20–26).
  **Counts here are not only about freeing. They are how the runtime knows a write may happen in
  place.** This is the crux of the design.
- **A query's answer is bytes.** `QueryDefinition.compute: fn(QueryEngine, Bytes) -> Bytes`
  (std-program query_engine.av:47). `computed_answer`, via `worked_out`, hashes those bytes and
  records them (query_engine.av:835–857). A reader decodes an answer into values of its own. So
  **nothing a query made is reachable from another query except through those bytes, or through
  state that outlives the query** (engine tables, the store's pending segments, `Cell`s, arenas
  and memo tables a query grows, `once` cells).

## 1. How a box knows it is region-held

Recommended: a REGION BIT in the header's flags byte, plus the region's DEPTH in the header's
16-bit stamp field. The kind stays the box's shape, unchanged.

- `kind_word` is low byte kind, then flags, then a 16-bit stamp (avra_box.h:47). The flags byte has
  room: bit 0 is OBSERVED, and 0xFF marks static data. A region box sets `REGION` (bit 1). Its
  stamp holds the region's depth: 1 for the outermost query a process computes, +1 for each query
  asked inside it. The stamp field is currently the write-observation turn number; that use moves
  to a side table for region boxes, or region boxes are left unobserved. That's a decision for
  stage 1, whose cost is measured there.
- Not an address range. Region pages would come from one reserved virtual range, so "is region"
  would be one compare on the pointer with no header load. But the DEPTH, which section 3 needs,
  would then need per-depth ranges or a page table lookup, and a promoted-in-place box (section 2)
  would sit in a region page while being heap. The header bit handles both. The range test stays
  available as a debug cross-check (section 4).
- Not a new negative kind. Retain and release would get the no-op for free, but section 0's crux
  says a region box must still answer "am I unique?" until the compiler can prove it (stage 2).
  The negative-kind trick is the stage-2 end state, for boxes the compiler licenses (section 5).

Retain and release in stage 1: a region box is COUNTED as now (`rc++` / `rc--`), so `rc == 1`
still licenses in-place writes. What changes is that **a region box reaching 0 is not freed and does
not cascade**: its memory goes back when the region ends. Freeing is where the expensive work is.
`reclaims` is 832 M on check-cli; each reclaim walks its slots, releasing children, and pushes onto a
free list. All of that work leaves. The increments stay until stage 2.

The new fast-path cost: release reads the flags byte when `rc` reaches 0, which is the rare,
out-of-line path. Retain is unchanged.

## 2. Escape points, and how each moves a value out

Stores of a pointer are the only way a region box can outlive its region. Two directions:
- **Heap (or an older region) → this region's box.** This is an ESCAPE, and must not leave a
  pointer into the region.
- **This region's box → heap.** This is a REMEMBERED pointer: the heap box's count was raised when
  it was stored, and must be released when the region ends, because a region box that dies does
  not cascade.

The escape points, in the order wrong-answers ranked them:

| Escape | Where | How it moves out | Cost given the top sites |
|---|---|---|---|
| The answer | `compute` returns `Bytes` (query_engine.av:47) | **Allocate in the target**: the answer writer (`SavedLayoutWriter`, whose `finished` is a top site) allocates its output buffer in the counted heap from the start, so the returned box is never region-held. No copy. | Zero copy. One flag on the writer's allocation. |
| Store segments | `Segment.keep`, the store's pending writes | Allocate in the target: the store's own buffers are heap. Bytes written into them are copied by value already (octets). | Zero beyond today's memcpy. |
| Tapes, arenas, memo tables a query grows | `SyntaxArena.placed_span`, `texts_of`, per-file tapes kept past the query | A **write barrier on slot and list stores**: storing a region pointer into a box of a lower depth (or into the heap) **promotes** it. Small boxes are deep-copied into the target's depth. Large boxes, and any subgraph past a size bound, are **promoted in place**: their REGION bit is cleared, their pages pinned, and the region keeps those pages at its end. | Copy cost proportional to escaped bytes. wrong-answers' 9.7% of boxes, 11% of bytes, are the ceiling, and most of those are answers and segments, which cost nothing above. The barrier itself costs a flags-byte compare on every pointer store. |
| `array_clone` (4.66 M) | Clones of shared values written | A clone made inside a region is a region box, unless its target slot is lower-depth, in which case the barrier promotes it. | Mostly stays in-region. |
| Engine tables (`settled_answers`, read sets, `lent`, frontier learned) | QueryEngine fields, `Cell`s and `HashKeyedTable`s | Their values are ContentHashes and bytes: scalars and heap octets. The barrier covers any boxed value. | Small. |
| `once` cells | `once fn` answers | Written once, live for the process. A `once` body computes under depth 0 (the heap), not in any region. | None. |

Promotion is deep: a promoted box's children that are region boxes are promoted too, by the same
copy-or-pin rule. Pin-in-place keeps addresses stable, so no pointer fix-up is ever needed. That
is why it is preferred for anything past the copy bound.

## 3. Nesting, and work-ahead forks

- **Regions form a stack per process**, keyed by depth. `computed_answer` pushes a region before
  `worked_out` and pops it after. A query asked while another computes gets depth d+1.
- **The rule is "point down, never up"**: a box may hold pointers to boxes of the same or lower
  depth (lower means older, including the heap at 0). The barrier compares the stored value's
  depth with the target's and promotes on a store that would point up. An outer query's values
  handed down as arguments are read freely by the inner query, since they outlive it. An inner
  query storing into an outer value, for example through a `Cell` it was handed, promotes to the
  outer depth.
- **Inner answers cross as bytes** (section 0). An outer query never holds an inner region's box,
  so popping a region frees it whole, with no scan.
- **Popping a region:**
  1. Release the remembered pointers (this region → heap or older region).
  2. Return every page that holds no pinned box.
  3. Fold pinned pages into the depth they were promoted to.
  The remembered set is appended to by the barrier, so its cost is proportional to the stores that
  made it.
- **Work-ahead forks:** `fork` copies the region stack along with memory. A worker computes its own
  queries under fresh regions, pushed above whatever the parent held at the fork, and hands
  results back through the store as bytes (`avra_pool_forked` already resets pool accounting at a
  fork, runtime/avra_pool.c:71). No region spans processes, and a forked child never pops a region
  it inherited. It exits.

## 4. What proves no region box survives its region

Layered, each catching what the one before can miss:

1. **Construction.** Answers and segments are allocated in their target (section 2), so the main
   escapes never create a region pointer to begin with.
2. **The write barrier**, in every build: every pointer store compares depths, then promotes. This
   is the runtime's soundness rule; nothing else is relied on.
3. **The debug region guard** (`AVRA_REGION_GUARD=1`): popping a region poisons its returned pages
   (`mprotect PROT_NONE`) instead of reusing them, so any surviving pointer traps on its first use.
   That's the same discipline as `AVRA_RC_GUARD`'s quarantine, applied to whole pages. A
   whole-heap scan for pointers into the popped address range, a debug-only and expensive pass, is
   a second check at region pop on a sample of queries.
4. **The memory pass**, statically: it already proves which values a body owns, lends or hands back
   (the lent and consumed marks). It learns one more fact per store: the depth of the target, which
   the program layer knows (a field of a value made in this query, against one handed in, a `Cell`,
   an engine table). Then a store the barrier would have to promote is flagged at compile time, as
   cost, and as a cue to allocate in the target.
5. **The RC guard and the soundness check** keep running unchanged over all of it. A region box
   still has a real count in stage 1, so their invariants still hold.

## 5. Expected census delta, and a staged plan where each stage is measurable alone

Base: cold `check packages/cli` (816 M boxes; 2.09 G retains, 2.92 G releases, 832 M reclaims on
the cost snapshot a6d0d0a0).

| Stage | What lands | Measured by | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0. Count it** | Census only. Every box records the depth it was made at, and its death whether it died at that depth. This is wrong-answers' measurement, made a permanent census row: `region: died-home N / escaped M by site`. | The census itself | Today's 90.3% / 9.7%, as a row. |
| **1. Regions own memory, counts stay** | The depth stack in `computed_answer`, the region bump allocator (page-sized arenas), the flags bit and depth stamp, the write barrier with promote (copy or pin), the remembered set, pop. A region box reaching 0 doesn't free. | `reclaims`, the free-list and cascade time, cold check-cli wall time and peak RSS, plus two new rows: `promoted boxes / bytes` and `barrier promotions by site`. | Reclaims −85..−90% (832 M → ~100 M). Retains and releases unchanged. Allocation goes from free-list to bump. Peak may rise, since a region frees at its end, not as boxes die. That is bounded by the largest query's working set and must be measured. |
| **2. Allocate in the target** | `SavedLayoutWriter` and the store's segment buffers allocate in the heap. The barrier's top promotion sites from stage 1 are each made to allocate in their target. | `promoted bytes` falls; wall time | Most of the stage-1 promotion bytes gone. Only the tapes and arenas that genuinely outlive their query still promote. |
| **3. Licensed uncounted** | The memory pass marks values proven unique, region-local and never stored down. Their boxes are made with the region's immortal-shape kind (−(k+4) with the REGION bit), so retain and release are the existing one-compare no-op. A write through one is in place by license, not by `rc == 1`. | `retains` and `releases` | Up to −58% of retains and releases (wrong-answers' share on boxes that die home), less whatever the pass can't prove unique. Each license is a row, so the census names what it proved. |
| **4. Retire per-read lending** | If stage 3 removes what lent/Grown targets, lent-59's per-read lending is kept only where a view crosses region boundaries. | The census, against lent-59 parked | Decided by the numbers, not ahead of them. |

Each stage lands alone, with its own census before and after and the existing soundness receipts:
sound check 0, RC guard clean, eval == native, the edit gate. Stage 1 also needs the region guard
(section 4.3) clean over the full suite before it lands.

## Open questions, for whoever builds it

- Do OBSERVED and stamp-based write logging matter for region boxes, which no other query can see?
  If not, a region box simply isn't observed and the stamp is free for the depth.
- The pin threshold, copy versus pin-in-place: to set from stage 1's promotion-size histogram.
- Peak memory under stage 1, for the largest queries (whole-package walks). If one query's working
  set is the problem, a query may sub-region its own loops: the memory pass knows loop-local values
  as well. That's a later step, not part of this design.

<to_controller>Lent/Grown time-box. The per-caller census found where the −5 % went: cli build, before 2,324,674,226 retains, after 2,328,927,538.
- **Where it went:** `Arena.node_at` now reads its element as a view (`avra_array_get`, 173.9 M times, against `_owned` 173.2 M before). But its caller store.expr (`SyntaxArena.expr` / `.stmt`) takes `avra_grown_view_owned`, the owned twin. So the 173 M retains moved up one level instead of disappearing.
- **Cause:** a caller that returns a grown read never lends it on. That's true on both the name-matching and the mark compiler, shown with a Grown<Book> `book_at` and its caller, so the bug is older than the mark change. `answer_chain` refuses any register whose layout carries a cell unless the body is itself a grown read (memory.av:1525). The holder seat a lend-through reaches always carries cells, so store.expr's chain dies at `self.exprs`.
- **The +0.7 % boxes and list reads:** these follow from it. The lent rewrite inserts its view rows (`avra_grown_view_owned` per read), adding list reads and boxes on 173 M node reads that buy nothing back.
- **Quick fix, uncommitted in /work/avra:** a cell is allowed past an outlasting lend (`&& !beyond`). The `past` registers are reached only through `lent_through`, whose lending map holds grown reads only.
- **Running now:** gen-1 with the fix, the book_at/through_length IR (book_at should lend, through_length should read a grown view), and native == eval.
- **Then:** if it holds, the full receipts again (2–3 h). If not, I park lent-59 at 2a275ddf with these numbers.
Also: /work/regions-design.md is written and was uploaded.</to_controller>

static void report_labelled_sites(const char* name, Site* tbl, int limit, intptr_t slide) {
    Site* rows = malloc(sizeof(Site) * (size_t)(SITES / 2 + 1));
    if (!rows) return;
    int64_t n = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < SITES; i++) if (tbl[i].site && tbl[i].made > 0) rows[n++] = tbl[i];
    qsort(rows, (size_t)n, sizeof(Site), by_made_first);
    for (int64_t i = 0; i < n && i < limit; i++) {
        avra_say("%s: site %p %lld %lldB %s\n", name, (void*)((char*)rows[i].site - slide), (long long)rows[i].made,
                (long long)rows[i].count, rows[i].sample ? (const char*)rows[i].sample : "-");
    }
    free(rows);
}

static int by_label(const void* a, const void* b) {
    return strcmp((const char*)((const Site*)a)->site, (const char*)((const Site*)b)->site);
}

static int by_made_first(const void* a, const void* b) {
    int64_t x = ((const Site*)a)->made, y = ((const Site*)b)->made;
    return x < y ? 1 : x > y ? -1 : 0;
}

### 2026-11-20T11:19:59 AGENT
The measurement is done, and its main finding is that typing and lowering are already close to one walk per item:
- **Typing:** each body is typed once (`typed_fn` or `method_body_typed`).
- **Lowering:** one lowering per generic instance.

The extra per-item walks in those two phases are small:
- **item_refusals:** walks each typed body again for refused seats and unbound names, after typing has seen every node. 2.47 CPU-s on a build, 1.79 on a check.
- **written_typed:** 13,807 asks, almost all of them a wrapper around `typed_fn`, so pure engine overhead. 1.39 CPU-s.
- **receiver_use and surveyed:** walk method bodies for their receiver use. 0.94 + 0.71 CPU-s.

The large multi-walk costs sit elsewhere: laws, at 39 + 9.6 CPU-s, which is laws-fusion's; and lowering per generic instance, which is specialization, not fusion. So in typing and lowering, row 6's real target is about 5 CPU-s on a cold build, the bottom of its −5..−10 estimate.

<to_controller>Row 6 measured, before any design (cold cli; check traced with Q ask; build via bodies_wave with all families). No family computes the same question twice. Per item and phase:
- **Typing (16.5 CPU-s on build):** one walk per body already. `typed_fn` 7.95 s / 16,326, `method_body_typed` 7.17 s / 12,821. The extra per-item passes over the same nodes in this phase:
  - `item_refusals`: re-walks the typed body for refused seats and unbound names. 2.47 s / 22,861.
  - `written_typed`: a wrapper question per fn, 12,862 of 13,807 reaching `typed_fn`. 1.39 s, all engine.
  - `receiver_use` and `surveyed`: method-body walks for receiver use. 0.94 + 0.71 s.
- **Lowering (34.3 CPU-s):** one walk per generic instance. `lowered_under` 17.0 s / 17,240 and `lowered_method_under` 14.8 s / 13,208, against about 29 k bodies typed, so the extra asks are instances, not re-walks. `body_facts` (2.46 s / 32,485) reads the lowered unit, not nodes. `cost_remarks` is law-only.
- **Laws:** `law_findings` 39 s plus per-item 9.6 s (`item_fact_found`, `item_syntax_found`, `item_instances_checked`, `item_broken`): three per-item queries over each item, laws-fusion's.
- **Parse (check):** 38,336 distinct `item_tape` keys for 22,861 law items, 36 k of them from `file_abouts`. These are distinct text and context pairs, so not re-parses; whether some are one item under two contexts I can't tell from hashes. Worth a probe; not row 6.

Design (to build only on your go):
1. Fuse in typing: one question per body yields a TypedBody with parts. Part `types` is per-node types (today's typed_fn); part `refused` is refused seats plus unbound names, collected while typing, not by re-walking (today's item_refusals); part `receiver` is what a method does to its receiver (today's receiver_use, its survey).
2. `written_typed` becomes the same question keyed on the written item. The wrapper case still types its wrapper under the fn's name; it's no longer a separate ask.
3. Warm cutoff: readers read a PART (answer_parts' PartSeen), never the whole. Lowering reads `types`, laws read `refused`, writes-analysis reads `receiver`. An edit that changes only refusals (a name unbound) doesn't re-lower; one that changes only types doesn't re-run the refusal laws. Re-run work per edit kind stays as today, and the gate's per-kind counts show it.
4. The read set is unchanged: the fused query reads exactly the union of the three it replaces, all names this item's typing already reads.
5. Lowering: no fusion. It already walks once per instance; fewer instances would come from lowering generics once (a different design). `body_facts` stays a read of the lowered unit.
6. Expected: about −4.5..−5.5 CPU-s cold on build (refusals 2.5, wrapper asks 1.4, receiver walks 0.9–1.6), and fewer asks per warm body edit (3 → 1 typing-phase asks). Gated by the warm counts per kind, the edit witness, and the bodies-wave table before and after.
7. Risk: `receiver_use` is asked before a caller's typing; a recursion through receivers needs that part without the whole typing. If parts can't be asked ahead, it stays separate, and the gain is 3.9 s.
8. Bigger lever, not row 6: laws (49 CPU-s) are laws-fusion's, and the generic-instance re-lowering (~30 % of lowering asks) would be a design of its own.</to_controller>

export fn receiver_use(
    engine: QueryEngine,
    file: SourceFileAddress,
    owner: string,
    method: string,
    reader: string,
) -> ReceiverUse {
    let start = MethodAt { file: file, owner: owner, name: method, reader: reader }
    mut reached = [start]
    mut seen: Map<string, bool> = {}
    seen.set(method_key(start), true)
    mut at = 0
    while at < reached.length {
        let found = surveyed(engine, reached[at])
        if found.writes() { return ReceiverUse.Written }
        for m in found.reached {
            if seen.has(method_key(m)) { continue }
            seen.set(method_key(m), true)
            reached.push(m)
        }
        at = at + 1
    }
    let unproved? = reached.find_map((m) -> surveyed(engine, m).unproved) else { return ReceiverUse.Read }
    ReceiverUse.Unproved(unproved)
}

`receiver_use` settles condition 7. It isn't a walk of one body: it's a closure across methods. It surveys each method it reaches through the receiver, possibly in other items, so its answer can't be a part of one body's typing. It stays separate.

So the build is:
- **(a)** `typed_fn`'s answer in parts, `types` and `refused`, with `item_refusals` reading only `refused`.
- **(b)** `written_typed` stops being its own question. Today it copies `typed_fn`'s whole answer into a saved answer of its own, 13,807 times. It becomes a plain fn that asks `typed_fn`, and only a wrapped body keeps a question of its own.

Telling the lead, then reading `TypedBody` and every reader of `typed_fn`, `written_typed` and `method_body_typed`. Each reader must say which part it needs.

export fn wrapping(
    engine: QueryEngine,
    file: SourceFileAddress,
    name: string,
    method: MethodSite? = null,
) -> Wrapping {
    let made = body_generated(engine, file, name, method)
    let wrap? = made.items.find(it.wraps) else { return Wrapping { wrapper: null, said: made.said } }
    let tape = wrap.wrapper ?? wrap.tape
    let store = new_node_store()
    let stmts = item_read_back(store, PlacedTape { start: 0, tape: tape })
    Wrapping {
        wrapper: ReadItem { store: store, stmts: stmts, written: store.expr_count() },
        said: made.said,
    }
}

/// What the generators the fn `file` writes as `name` wears make, or with `method` those the method
/// of that name the impl writes wears.
fn body_generated(engine: QueryEngine, file: SourceFileAddress, name: string, method: MethodSite?) -> GeneratedItems {
    if method == null { fn_generated(engine, file, name) } else { method_generated(engine, method!, name) }
}

/// Whether a wrap stands on the body of the fn `file` writes as `name`, or with `method` of the
/// method of that name the impl writes: what `wrapping` answers of it, its wrapper never read back.
export fn wraps_body(
    engine: QueryEngine,
    file: SourceFileAddress,
    name: string,
    method: MethodSite? = null,
) -> bool { body_generated(engine, file, name, method).items.any(it.wraps) }

Before writing (a), one more finding changes its expected value. `item_refusals` doesn't decode its bodies by itself. It reads them through `item_stated_bodies`, which holds a per-item view in the process: the item's typed bodies are decoded once and shared by every law reader of that item. Those readers include `law_findings` and `item_rules`, which need `types`. So in a cold run the whole `TypedBody` is decoded once per item whatever `item_refusals` asks for. A `found`-only read in `item_refusals` would remove no decode, and (a)'s cold gain predicts to about zero.

fn body_checked(
    engine: QueryEngine,
    file: SourceFileAddress,
    signed: SignedBody,
    meanings: bool,
    written: bool = false,
) -> Checking {
    let signing = Signing {
        engine: engine,
        file: file,
        type_params: signed.signature.type_params,
        self_type: signed.receiver,
        writer: written_by(signed.item.store, signed.stmt),
        bounds: signed.signature.bounds,
    }
    mut cx = checking(
        signed.item.store,
        program_of(engine, file, signing, written),
        signed.signature.answer,
    ) with { meanings: meanings, fnless: signed.fnless }
    if signed.receiver != null { cx.bind(RECEIVER, signed.receiver, true, true, BindSite.Receiver) }
    for j, p in signed.signature.params {
        if signed.receiver != null && p.name == RECEIVER { continue }
        cx
            .bind_seat(p.name, p.ty, p.mutable || p.state, p.settled, BindSite.Seat(j), p.state, p.unshared)
    }
    for c in signed.consts { cx.bind(c.name, c.ty) }
    if signed.want != null {
        let _ = cx.check(signed.body, signed.want!)
        return cx
    }
    let seat = signed.seat ?? Seating.Body(signed.item.store.fn_parts(signed.stmt)?.name ?? "")
    let before = cx.refused.get().length
    let answered = cx.check_seated(signed.body, signed.signature.answer, seat)
    if signed.seat == null && cx.refused.get().length == before { cx.answers_nothing(signed.body, signed.signature.answer, answered, seat) }
    cx
}

/// The enum `ty` is: its type parameters and its variants, typed where it's declared. Absent for a
/// type that isn't an enum the program declares.
fn enum_shape(engine: QueryEngine, ty: SignedType) -> EnumShape? {
    let at? = declared_at(ty) else { return null }
    let declared? = enum_signature(engine, at.file, at.name) else { return null }
    EnumShape { params: declared.type_params.length, variants: declared.variants }
}

impl Checking {
    /// `e` checked against `expected`, its type kept.
    mut fn check(e: ExprId, expected: Expected) -> SignedType? {
        let outer = self.site
        self.site = BindSite.Expr(e.index)
        let refused_before = self.refused.get().length
        let meant = if self.meanings { self.store.meant(e) } else { null }
        self.seat_kept(e, expected)
        let made = if meant != null { self.meaning_checked(e, meant!, expected) } else { self.store.expr(e).checked(self, e, expected) }
        // a type the body decides is known only once typing infers it
        let ty = if made != null && made!.inferred() { null } else { made }
        if ty != null {
            self.types.set_at(e.index, ty)
            if self.refused.get().length == refused_before || fnless_wanted(expected, ty!) { self.agreed(e, expected, ty!) }
        }
        self.site = outer
        ty
    }

    /// What `e`, whose meaning is `meant`, is: what its meaning is; an instance its component judges
    /// is the literal under the `check` call its meaning makes, that call checked as a value of its own.
    mut fn meaning_checked(e: ExprId, meant: ExprId, expected: Expected) -> SignedType? {
        let value = self.store.instance_value(e)
        if value == null || self.store.checked_by(e) == null { return self.check(meant, self.store.expr(e).meaning_expected(expected)) }
        let _ = self.check(meant, Expected.Free)
        self.type_of(value!)
    }

### 2026-11-20T14:35:42 AGENT
Here's how core typing's 4.70 s splits:
- **Bodies with no meaning (5,236 of 16,848):** 55,128 nodes, 0.36 s. Here core typing is exactly a repeat of the surface typing, but these bodies are small.
- **Bodies with meanings (11,612):** 4.34 s. 38.7 % of their nodes sit outside any meaning and are typed again as the surface typed them; the rest sit inside meant subtrees. 27,495 substitution sites expand to 433,845 nodes checked, about 16 per site.

So the real cost is elaboration's output size, not the second walk as such. The probe is removed; /work/avra-v is clean.

<to_controller>Core-mode re-typing, measured (cold cli build, 16,848 core-mode bodies, 4.70 s), with a design verdict:
1. **What core mode adds:** core typing is surface typing with meant subtrees checked in place of their written nodes (checking.av:1010), and about 15 surface-only law checks skipped. 27,495 substitution sites expand to 433,845 nodes checked inside meanings, 56.8 % of all nodes core mode checks, about 16 nodes per site.
2. **What is a pure repeat:** bodies with no meaning (5,236, 31 %) cost only 0.36 s. In bodies with meanings, 38.7 % of nodes lie outside any meaning and are re-typed identically. That's the most a "meanings pass over surface facts" could save: ≤1.7 s, node-proportional.
3. **Why not a meanings pass:** at each meant site it would need the checker's scope, expected type and flow facts from the surface walk. TypedBody would have to record them, and the pass would have to reproduce core typing exactly. That's a larger representation and more risk than ≤1.7 s buys.
4. **Why not typing meanings inside the surface walk:** that saves about 1.7 s per build, but adds about 2.6 s (the inside-meaning work) to every check, which never lowers. That trades cold check for cold build, so no.
5. **Warm:** unmoved either way. Lowering already re-runs exactly when the body's typing does.
6. **Verdict:** don't build. The only safe piece is lowering reading typed_fn for meaning-free bodies, 0.36 s, not worth it alone. The real lever is meanings' size, the ~16× expansion of sugar into meant trees (string interpolation, comprehensions, match sugar). Typing a sugar node directly, or elaborating less, would shrink both core typing and lowering. That's a lowering-quality design question, not row 6.
Probe removed; /work/avra-v is clean. Ready for the next item.</to_controller>

//! What an `if` means, in the core.
use core.{At}
use features.{TypedCode, meaning, typed_coded}

/// `if c { a } else { b }` is a match on the condition; without an else, the other arm does nothing.
export meaning if_else {
    quote { if ${c} { ${..taken} } else { ${..other} } } -> quote {
        match ${c} {
            true -> {
                ${taken}
            }
            _ -> {
                ${other}
            }
        }
    },
    quote { if ${c} { ${..taken} } } if elseless(it) -> quote {
        match ${c} {
            true -> {
                ${taken}
            }
            _ -> {
                ${nothing_in(it)}
            }
        }
    },
}

/// Whether the `if` has no else.
fn elseless(subject: TypedCode) -> bool {
    match subject.at {
        .Expr(e) -> match subject.of.view.store.expr(e) { .If(_, _, other) -> other == null, rest -> false },
        .Stmt(_) or .Pat(_) or .Field(_, _) or .Param(_, _) -> false,
    }
}

/// No statements, in the item `subject` stands in.
fn nothing_in(subject: TypedCode) -> List<TypedCode> { typed_coded(subject.of, []) }

//! The lowering rule of an `if` no meaning takes — one whose `else` is another `if`: a region on the
//! condition, its block in one arm and its `else` in the other.
use core.{ExprId, Lowering, Lowers, Reg, SignedType, owned_type}
use core.expr.{If}

impl Lowers for If {
    /// A region of the `if`'s type on the condition: the block where it holds, else the `else`, or
    /// nothing where there's none.
    fn lowered(mut cx: Lowering, e: ExprId) -> Reg {
        let ty? = cx.type_at(e) else { return cx.unlowered(e) }
        cx
            .region(cx.lower(self.cond), cx.laid_out(ty)) { cx -> branch(cx, self.on_true, ty) } else { cx -> branch_or_nothing(cx, self.on_false, ty) }
    }

    /// A region on the condition whose arms are run for what they do.
    fn lowered_dropped(mut cx: Lowering, e: ExprId) -> Reg {
        cx
            .void_branches(cx.lower(self.cond)) { cx -> let _ = cx.dropped(self.on_true) } else { cx -> if self.on_false != null { let _ = cx.dropped(self.on_false!) } }
        cx.hollow_of(owned_type("void"))
    }
}

/// A branch's value, or where it leaves, nothing of the `if`'s type `ty`.
fn branch(mut cx: Lowering, x: ExprId, ty: SignedType) -> Reg {
    let made = cx.lower(x)
    if cx.store.leaves(x) { cx.hollow_of(ty) } else { made }
}

/// The `else`'s value, or where there's none or it leaves, nothing of the `if`'s type `ty`.
fn branch_or_nothing(mut cx: Lowering, x: ExprId?, ty: SignedType) -> Reg {
    let v? = x else { return cx.hollow_of(ty) }
    branch(cx, v, ty)
}

    fn kids() -> List<ExprId> { [self.cond] }

/// nothing. Empty for an `if` whose condition binds nothing.
fn payload_match(store: SyntaxArena, cond: ExprId, taken: ExprId, other: ExprId?, span: Span?) -> List<
    ExprId,
> {
    let payload? = store.is_payload(cond) else { return [] }
    let rest = store.alloc_pat(Pat.Wild, span)
    let arms = [

6. **Risk:** generated code. A region against a match on a bool should give the same native branch.
